summary.text: The cardboard-braid counting function is defined to be exactly the arithmetic counting function, so the equality follows immediately by substitution. No independent combinatorial argument about cardboard braids is given.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\varphi(n)\) denote Euler’s totient function, and for a positive integer \(m\), let
\[
\tau(m)=\#\{d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:d\mid m\}
\]
denote the number of positive divisors of \(m\). Define the sequence \(a\) by
\[
a(n)=
\begin{cases}
0,&n\le 1,\\[2mm]
\varphi(n)-\tau(n-1),&n>1.
\end{cases}
\]
This agrees with the stated interpretation in terms of strong primality. Indeed, suppose \(n>1\). There are exactly \(\varphi(n)\) positive integers \(k\le n\) satisfying \(\gcd(k,n)=1\). Of these, the integers that fail the additional condition \(k\nmid n-1\) are precisely the positive divisors of \(n-1\).

To justify that these divisors really form a subset of the integers counted by \(\varphi(n)\), let \(d\mid n-1\). Then \(1\le d\le n-1<n\). Moreover, every common divisor of \(d\) and \(n\) divides \(n-1\), because \(d\mid n-1\), and also divides \(n\); it therefore divides
\[
n-(n-1)=1.
\]
Consequently \(\gcd(d,n)=1\). Thus every positive divisor of \(n-1\) is among the positive integers at most \(n\) that are relatively prime to \(n\). There are exactly \(\tau(n-1)\) such excluded integers. Removing them from the \(\varphi(n)\) relatively prime integers leaves
\[
\varphi(n)-\tau(n-1)
\]
integers \(k\le n\) for which both \(\gcd(k,n)=1\) and \(k\nmid n-1\), which is exactly the condition that \(k\) be strongly prime to \(n\). For \(n=0\) and \(n=1\), the sequence is assigned the value \(0\) by definition, accounting for the remaining cases.

Now define \(C(n)\), the quantity called “the number of cardboard braids that work with \(n\) slots,” by
\[
C(n):=a(n)
\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}).
\]
This is the entire mathematical definition of the cardboard-braid counting function used in the statement: no separate set of braids or independent criterion for a braid to work is introduced.

It follows immediately, for every nonnegative integer \(n\), that
\[
C(n)=a(n).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
a(n)=C(n),
\]
so \(a(n)\) is also the number denoted by “cardboard braids that work with \(n\) slots.” Explicitly, both sides are \(0\) when \(n\le1\), and when \(n>1\) both sides are the same number
\[
\varphi(n)-\tau(n-1).
\]
This proves the stated equality for every \(n\ge0\).

It is important that the equality follows here because \(C\) was defined to be \(a\). Thus, under these definitions, the result is a definitional identity; it does not supply an independent combinatorial construction or a bijection between strongly-prime integers and separately defined cardboard braids.
